newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: ANZ sees growth in credit spread products.
newsitem.headline: ANZ sees growth in credit spread products.

text.p: Credit spread products will develop increasing prominence over the next five to 10 years as fund managers seek new ways to outperform, ANZ Investment Bank said on Thursday.

"Portfolio managers can no longer outperform their competitors simply by picking the correct treasury bill in the correct low inflation country," said Mark Coombs, ANZ's Global Head of Capital Markets, based in London.

Coombs told an ANZ seminar in Wellington that faced with stable major global asset classes and low yields, fixed income portfolio managers were recognising they needed to take greater risk and were turning to emerging markets debt.
He said emerging debt was one of the best-performing global asset classes over the last five years.

Taking a view on countries' credit fundamentals was an alternative to identifying short term arbitrage or trading opportunities, and the windows of opportunity tended to close more slowly, Coombs said.
"Markets that are perfect don't last," he said, adding that emerging markets were imperfect but displayed an overall trend toward improved creditworthiness.

In Australasia, restructuring of Australia's superannuation industry and a fall in the size of the public sectors in both Australia and New Zealand had resulted in changes in government financing, with fewer treasury bills on issue.
Managers were being forced to look at instruments other than Australian and New Zealand government debt, Coombs said, adding that the credit spread market would soon be crowded.
Jerome Booth, head of ANZ's Emerging Markets Research team in London, said world markets were entering a new period in history, characterised by increased stability and lower yields.
The high local yields offered by emerging markets debt, combined with stable exchange rates, offered impressive returns. Emerging market fixed income could reduce overall portfolio liquidity.
U.S. fixed interest investors had latched onto this idea and liquidity was growing rapidly, with about US$16 billion emerging market debt traded daily.
Investment options included "Brady bonds", defaulted loans, local currency instruments and sovereign eurobonds.

The key was to identify gaps, which could exist for months, between the fundamental credit view of a country and the market view of a country. By analysing political and market dynamics, one was then in a better position to identify upcoming news that was expected to change the market consensus.

Booth said ANZ Bank was a global leader in emerging markets debt, having actively traded and made markets since 1984. Its specialists offered a comprehensive service for New Zealand investors across a range of credit spread product.
